title: Quantum Nonlocal Games on Graph Ensembles
authors: Joshua Tucker, Chris Weeks, Peter Drmota, Ellis M. Ainley, Ayush Agrawal, Adam R. Martinez, Erin Malinowski, Jacob A. Blackmore, David P. Nadlinger, Gabriel Araneda, David M. Lucas, Carlos A. Perez-Delgado, Paul Strange, Jorge Quintanilla
abstract: Quantum entanglement is one of the most striking discoveries in all of science. This effect allows, for instance, two spatially separated agents to coordinate their actions, without communication, to an extent that is both counter-intuitive, and provably impossible by any other physical means. A recently discovered example is that of mobile agents (players) performing spatial coordination tasks such as rendezvous, where the agents aim to meet on a network without communication. Until now, demonstrations of this advantage have relied on highly idealized conditions: agents are assumed to have complete knowledge of the topography, and experiments have been restricted to simulations using data generated by qubits within a single quantum processor. Here we address both limitations by developing a theory for graph ensembles that capture topographical uncertainty and by experimentally demonstrating the advantage in rendezvous scenarios between physically separated ion-trap systems with access to remote entanglement. Moreover, we simulate a broader set of problems on superconducting hardware. Surprisingly, when players are given the ability to gather more local information the quantum advantage increases -- a feat impossible by classical means. Our findings establish a concrete route toward practical quantum advantages in motion coordination problems. More broadly, they point to a new way of using portable quantum devices to enhance collective decision-making in uncertain environments.
summary: This work establishes a concrete route toward achieving quantum advantage in motion coordination problems by analyzing nonlocal games played on graphs with unknown topographies. The authors demonstrate this theoretically using graph ensembles and experimentally validate it using physically separated trapped ion systems. Crucially, they show that the quantum benefit persists under topographical uncertainty and is significantly amplified when players can gather local information.
main_problem: The research investigates when quantum entanglement provides a demonstrable advantage over classical strategies for coordinating mobile agents (players) in uncertain environments defined by graph ensembles.
main_result: Quantum strategies maintain and even enhance their advantage over optimal classical ones, particularly when players gain access to additional local information about the environment's topography.
method: The authors develop theoretical frameworks for nonlocal quantum games on graph ensembles and validate them through experimental demonstrations using trapped ion systems and simulations on superconducting hardware.
model_or_system: The core model involves two-player, one-step rendezvous or domination games played on graphs drawn from an ensemble. Experimentally, the platform uses physically separated trapped $^{88}	ext{Sr}^+$ ions to generate remote entanglement.
key_observables: Quantum Advantage ($Q$), Rendezvous Probability ($P_W$), and Graph Ensemble Entropy ($S$).
important_parameters: Topographic Uncertainty (Entropy $S$), the availability of local information ('signposts'), and the specific graph ensembles used ($\{C_3, C_5\}, \{C_3, C_6\}$, etc.).
main_assumptions: The classical strategy is assumed to be deterministic; quantum strategies rely on shared maximally entangled 2-qubit states and local unitary rotations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of Quantum Advantage ($Q$) versus Ensemble Entropy ($S$), comparing scenarios with and without additional local information, across different graph ensembles for both rendezvous and domination games.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the nonlocal game on uncertain graphs to demonstrating quantum advantage in the rendezvous scenario using trapped ions. It then extends this analysis to the graph domination game, consistently showing that increased local knowledge boosts the quantum benefit.
why_interesting: The experimental realization of remote entanglement and its application to complex coordination tasks like rendezvous is highly relevant for developing practical quantum networking protocols and understanding how quantum correlations can enhance collective decision-making in noisy or uncertain physical settings.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The games we consider involve two agents, Alice and Bob, coordinating their moves on a graph in order to achieve a common task. They are played in two phases: in phase one (a) Alice and Bob can agree a strategy and share quantum information without knowing their starting locations and with only statistical information about the graph’s topology; in phase two (b-d) Alice and Bob have to make their moves without communicating and using only local information (see main text).

FIG. 2. (a) The experimental apparatus used to implement rendezvous games on graph ensembles consists of two trapped 88Sr+ ions. The ions can be entangled remotely by a Bell state measurement (BSM) on two photons that are each entangled with one of the ions. The BSM heralds the creation of the state in Eq. (3) whose phase ϑγ is communicated to Bob. The variables x and y encode the sites at which Alice and Bob have been placed on the graph and the players perform unitary rotations and projective measurements using lasers, yielding binary outcomes a and b, respectively. (b) Relevant electronic level structure of 88Sr+.
